'''''Rhynchospora alba''''', the '''white beak-sedge''', is a plant in the sedge family, [[Cyperaceae]]. It is a tufted [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial]] around 50 cm tall, with white [[inflorescence]]s that flower in August.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Sedges of the British Isles. B.S.B.I. Handbook No. 1|last1=Jermy|first1=C|last2=Simpson|first2=D|last3=Foley|first3=M|last4=Porter|first4=M|publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles|year=2007|location=London}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Flora of North America|last=Kral|first=R|publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden Press|year=2002|volume=23|location=St Louis|pages=230–239}}</ref> The fruit of the sedge is a small [[achene]] with a characteristic beak-like cap. It is dispersed by wind or falls by gravity, leading to individuals existing in tight clumps. The species favours wet, acidic and nutrient poor soils, thriving in ''[[Sphagnum]]''-dominated bogs, but also [[peat]]y [[grassland]]s.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Ohlson|first1=M|last2=Malmer|first2=N|date=1990|title=Total Nutrient Accumulation and Seasonal Variation in Resource Allocation in the Bog Plant Rhynchospora alba|journal=Oikos|volume=58|issue=1|pages=100–108|doi=10.2307/3565365|jstor=3565365}}</ref> As such, it is often used as a positive indicator for bog and [[mire]] [[ecosystem health]].<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|last=Rynbníček|first=K|date=1970|title=Rhynchospora alba (L.) Vahl. Its Distribution, Communities and Habitat Conditions in Czechslovakia Part 1|journal=Folia Geobotanica & Phytotaxonomica|volume=5|issue=2|pages=145–162|doi=10.1007/BF02851823|s2cid=32046119}}</ref>

The species was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in 1753 under a different [[genus]] and name, ''Schoenus albus'',<ref name=":10">{{Cite book|title=Species Plantarum 1|last=Linnaeus|first=C|year=1753|pages=44}}</ref> but was subsequently reclassified into the novel genus ''[[Rhynchospora]]'' by [[Martin Vahl|Vahl]] in 1805.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=Enumerato Plantarum 2|last=Vahl|first=M.H.|year=1805|pages=229}}</ref> It has a wide range across the Northern Hemisphere, extending from the inland [[wetland]]s of [[North America]], across [[Europe]] to the [[Korean Peninsula]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":11">{{Cite journal|title=''Rhynchospora alba''. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2014|last=Matchutadze|first=I|date=2014|doi = 10.2305/IUCN.UK.2014-1.RLTS.T19618181A19620886.en|doi-access=free}}</ref> Due to this large range, there is considerable variation between populations, and numerous varieties have been identified.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web|url=https://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do;jsessionid=4B33FF97D5374717D7D08788175304B1.kppapp06-wcsp?name_id=261498|title=World Checklist of Cyperaceae: Sedges|last1=Govaerts|first1=R|last2=Simpson|first2=D.A.|date=2007}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Gale|first=S|date=1944|title=''Rhynchospora'' sect. ''Eurhynchospora'' in Canada, the United States and the West Indies.|journal=Rhodora|volume=46|pages=89–134}}</ref> The plant has few uses, though it is used as an ornamental in the [[United Kingdom|UK]].

==Description==
''Rhynchospora alba'' is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] herb between 10 and 50 cm in height,<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite book|title=Flora of China|last1=Wu|first1=Z.|last2=Raven|first2=P.H.|publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden Press|volume=23|location=St Louis|pages=1–515}}</ref> though plants up to 75 cm tall can be found in [[North America]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last=McMillan|first=P.D|date=2007|title=''Rhynchospora'' (Cyperaceae) of South Carolina and the Eastern United States|journal=Biota of South Carolina|volume=5|pages=1–269}}</ref> The plant grows in tight clumps, meaning it is often difficult to distinguish individual stems.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4" />

The plant consists of a single erect stem, which is three-angled and thin, usually 0.5–1 mm thick.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":6" /> The leaves attached to the stem are three-ranked (in spirals around the three edges of the stem) and [[Leaf|parallel veined]], extending up to 15 cm in length <sup>[6]</sup>, though none overtop the stem.<ref name=":1" /> Each leaf is differentiated into a green or straw coloured sheath, which hugs the stem, and a grey/green blade, which is flat and slender (0.7–2 mm) and tapers to a blunt tip.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5" /> In some specimens, the margins of the blade are sparsely covered in hairs.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> Unlike many [[Cyperaceae|sedge]] species, there is no [[ligule]] (outgrowths at the meeting of the blade and sheath).<ref name=":1" /> At the base of the plant, the leaves have no blade, and only the sheaths are present.<ref name=":0" /> These are often subtending a 10–20 mm bud, which will overwinter and grow a new plant in spring.<ref name=":2" />

While most ''[[Rhynchospora]]'' have large [[rhizome]]s (tuber-like stems below the soil surface), ''R. alba'' has very small rhizomes, or none at all, and very shallow root systems.<ref name=":5" /> This reflects its different life history to many other [[Cyperaceae|sedges]] – ''R. alba'' loses all but the basal overwintering bud during the winter, while most other species retain and store nutrients in well-developed rhizome and [[root]] structures.<ref name=":2" />

=== Reproductive structures ===
''Rhynchospora alba'' flowers in August,<ref name=":5" /> and these flowers are arranged into white [[inflorescence]]s in a hierarchy of units. Each individual flower is surrounded a white (or brown in older tissues), leaf-like structure called a '[[glume]]'.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book|title=The Families and Genera of Vascular Plants.|last=Goetghebeur|first=P.|publisher=Springer-Verlag|year=1998|editor-last=Kubitzki|editor-first=K.|location=Berlin|pages=141–190|chapter=Cyperaceae|editor-last2=Huber|editor-first2=H.|editor-last3=Rudall|editor-first3=P.J.|editor-last4=Stevens|editor-first4=P.S.|editor-last5=Stuetzel|editor-first5=T.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Holrrum|first=R.E.|date=1948|title=The Spikelet in Cyperaceae|journal=Botanical Review|volume=14|issue=8|pages=525–541|doi=10.1007/BF02861576|s2cid=30428671}}</ref> These glumes are grouped into egg-shaped '[[spikelet]]s' between 3 and 6 mm in length, and two to seven of these spikelets are clustered together into a hemispheric cluster, making the [[inflorescence]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5" /> As with many other ''Rhynchospora'', there are 4–5 glumes in each spikelet, with the bottom one or two glumes being sterile (they do not contain flowers) and the top three glumes alternating fertile, sterile, fertile.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> As such there are usually one or two flowers per spikelet. Most plants have between one and three inflorescences growing off the stem, each subtended by a short leaf-like [[bract]], about 2–3 x the length of the inflorescence.<ref name=":1" /> Each flower is [[Plant reproductive morphology|bisexual]], comprising a superior [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] with a bifurcating style and 2–3 [[anthers]] (each 1 mm in length).<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last=Kükenthal|first=G.|date=1949–1951|title=Vorarbeiten zu einer Monographie der Rhynchosporoideae|journal=Bot. Jahrb. Syst.|volume=74; 75|pages=375–509; 90–115, 273–314, 451–497}}</ref> The [[petal]]s and [[sepal]]s ([[perianth]]) are homogenous and highly modified, forming ring of 9–13 bristles with downward-facing barbs.<ref name=":0" />

After [[pollination]] the flower develops into an [[achene]] – a dry fruit that is indehiscent (it does not open at maturity) and contains a single seed.<ref name=":7" /> This is composed of a 2 mm x 1 mm, egg-shaped achene body and the remnants of the style base of the flower, which forms a 1 mm beak-like structure called the tubercle.<ref name=":6" /> The perianth bristles are also retained, and these are shorter than, or the same length as, the achene and tubercle combined.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> The lengths of both the tubercle and perianth bristles are key characters for distinguishing ''R. alba'' from other ''Rhynchospora'' species.<ref name=":6" />

=== Similar species ===
White beak-sedge closely resembles a number of other sedges, including the brown beak-sedge ([[Rhynchospora fusca|''R. fusca'']]) and large beak-sedge ([[Rhynchospora macra|''R. macra'']]).<ref name=":1" /> It can be distinguished from other species by the reduced size of its rhizomes, the length of the tubercle and perianth bristles on the fruit, and the presence of downward facing barbs on the bristles.<ref name=":0" />

==Etymology==
The genus ''Rhynchospora'' derives from the Greek ''Rhynkos'' – "beak" and ''spora'' "seed".<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6" /> This, along with the genus’ common name beak-sedge, refers to the long beak-like tubercle at the top of the achene fruit. This is characteristic to the entire genus and is often used for intra-generic classification.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":8" /> The species name ''alba'' derives from the Latin ''albus'', or white,<ref name=":6" /> and refers to the white glumes surrounding each flower, which give the inflorescence its colour.

The species has multiple common names, the most common being white beak-sedge, again referring to the inflorescence colour and shape of the tubercle.<ref name=":0" /> It is also known as white beak-rush, though this is misleading, as it is not in the rush family.

==Habitat and ecology==
''Rhynchospora alba'' favours [[acid]]ic, nutrient poor conditions and is found across a range of wetland environments.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":9" /><ref name=":5" /> It is most commonly found in [[ombrotrophic]] [[bog]]s (where plant nutrients are only obtained through rainfall and [[dry deposition]]) and ''[[Sphagnum]]'' moss-dominated communities, where it is one of the few [[vascular plant]] species present.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":9" /> Studies into nutrient and mass allocation by ''R. alba'' found the plant exhibits much higher rates of nutrient accumulation and loss across the growing season than in other sedges, which rely more heavily on storage and remobilising of nutrients in rhizomes.<ref name=":2" /> This is likely related to the much lower levels of [[interspecific competition]] experienced by ''R. alba'' in these bogs than other sedges in more grass-dominated environments.

It is also found in [[peatlands]] alongside other sedge species such as ''[[Carex]]'' species.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":9" /> It has a persistent [[seed bank]], with seeds living up to five years.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Egawa|first1=C.|last2=Koyana|first2=A.|last3=Tsuyuzaki|first3=S.|date=2009|title=Relationships between the development of seedbank, standing vegetation and litter in a post-mined peatland|journal=Plant Ecology|volume=200|issue=2|pages=217–228|doi=10.1007/s11258-008-9536-5|hdl=2115/38899|s2cid=1782787|hdl-access=free}}</ref> It is therefore often an early re-coloniser in disturbed environments, where it can become the dominant species in so-called ''R. alba'' sedgeland.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal|last1=Egawa|first1=C.|last2=Tsuyuzaki|first2=S.|date=2011|title=Seedling establishment of late colonizer is facilitated by seedling and overstory of early colonizer in a post-mined peatland.|journal=Plant Ecology|volume=212|issue=3|pages=369–381|doi=10.1007/s11258-010-9828-4|s2cid=26144449}}</ref> It is much less dominant of more established communities, however, as it is less capable of outcompeting sedge species with more developed root and rhizome systems.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":13" />

''Rhynchospora alba'' is [[Anemophily|wind-pollinated]] and wind-dispersed,<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7" /> so has few close interactions with [[Entomophily|insect pollinators]], but is a major food source for a number of bog-dwelling species, such as ''[[Paraphlepsius]]'' leafhoppers in the US.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chandler|first1=D.|last2=Hamilton|first2=K.|date=2017|title=Biodiversity and ecology of the leafhoppers (Hemiptera: Cicadellidae) of New Hampshire.|journal=Transactions of the American Entomological Society|volume=143|issue=4|pages=773–971|doi=10.3157/061.143.0408|s2cid=90424788}}</ref>

==Distribution==
Although most species of ''Rhynchospora'' are found in [[tropics]],<ref name=":8" /> ''R. alba'' is more restricted to the higher [[latitude]]s of the [[Northern Hemisphere]], where climatic conditions favour the establishment of [[bog]]s and fens.<ref name=":11" /><ref name=":7" /><ref name=":14">{{Cite journal|title=GBIF Backbone Taxonomy|url=https://www.gbif.org/dataset/d7dddbf4-2cf0-4f39-9b2a-bb099caae36c|doi=10.15468/39omei|year=2017|author1=Registry-Migration.Gbif.Org|type=Data Set|publisher=GBIF Secretariat}}</ref> It has a wide [[boreal climate|boreal]] distribution and is commonly found in the US (north of [[California]] and [[South Carolina]]<ref name=":6" />), [[Canada]], Europe, the [[Caucasus]], China, Japan and the [[Korean Peninsula]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":11" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":14" />

It is generally found at lower [[altitude]]s (below 850 m),<ref name=":1" /> but has been found at higher altitudes at the southern edge of its range, for example in China and [[Puerto Rico]].<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" />

==Taxonomy and systematics==
Owing to the high [[biodiversity]] and significant [[morphology (biology)|morphological]] similarity seen across the sedges, ''R. alba'' has a somewhat complex [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic]] history. The species was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753, and was classified in the same genus as [[bog rush]]es (due to similarities in inflorescence) under the binomial name ''[[Schoenus (plant)|Schoenus]] albus''.<ref name=":10" /> This classification proved inaccurate, and [[Martin Vahl|Martin Henrichsen Vahl]] reclassified the species in 1805 as ''Rhynchospora alba'', placing it in a novel genus that grouped species with a characteristic beak-like [[tubercle]] on the achene fruit.<ref name=":3" />

''Rhynchospora alba'' (L.) Vahl is the current accepted species name for the white beak-sedge, but there has been considerable contention around its classification over the last 200 years<ref name=":4" /> (see below). Neither Vahl nor Linnaeus provided specific [[Type (biology)|type specimens]] with their descriptions, but a recent typification of ''R. alba'' designated a specimen from Linnaeus' collection as a [[lectotype]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cafferty|first1=J.|last2=Jarvis|first2=C.E.|date=2004|title=Typification of Linnean Plant Names in Cyperaceae.|journal=Taxon|volume=53|issue=1|pages=177–181|doi=10.2307/4135509|jstor=4135509}}</ref>

=== Contention around ''Rhynchospora'' classification ===
The classification of ''R. alba'' has come under considerable scrutiny since Vahl's description, due to conflicting [[Biological classification|classification]]s of the genus ''Rhynchospora'' and closely related [[Taxon|taxa]].<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":7" /><ref name=":15">{{Cite journal|last1=Thomas|first1=W.W.|last2=Araujo|first2=A.C.|last3=Alves|first3=M.V.|date=2009|title=A Preliminary Molecular Phylogeny of the Rhynchosporae (Cyperaceae).|journal=Botanical Review|volume=75|issue=1|pages=22–29|doi=10.1007/s12229-008-9023-7|s2cid=13432358}}</ref> Vahl classified ''Rhynchospora'' based on the tubercle/fruit alone.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":15" /> Other taxonomists, such as [[Christian Gottfried Daniel Nees von Esenbeck|Nees]], only recognised species with bifid [[Style (botany)|styles]] as ''Rhynchospora'', and moved many species into 11 other [[Genus|genera]] (both novel and pre-existing), all within a wider group called the Rhynchosporae.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Nees von Esenheck|first=C.G.D.|date=1835|title=Uebersicht der Cyperaceengattungen (Synopsis Generum Cyperacearum)|journal=Linnaea|volume=9|pages=282–297}}</ref> [[George Bentham|Bentham]] and [[Joseph Dalton Hooker|Hooker]] tried to resolve this conflict by splitting ''Rhynchospora'' into two subgenera – ''Diplostylae'' and ''Haplostylae'' – based on the branching pattern of the [[Style (botany)|style]].<ref name=":15" /><ref>{{Cite book|title=Genera Plantarum|last1=Bentham|first1=G.|last2=Hooker|first2=J.D.|publisher=Lovell Reeve & Co.|year=1883|location=London|pages=1041}}</ref> This was only partially accepted, however, and many previously described genera, such as ''[[Dichromena]]'', were still used, sometimes even replacing ''Rhynchospora''.<ref name=":4" /> This persisted until Kükenthal published an extensive treatment of Rhynchosporae in 1949, and classified all 250 known [[species]] into either ''Rhynchospora'' or the closely related ''[[Pleurostachys]]'', with all other names either synonyms or sub-groups.<ref name=":8" /> Kükenthal also split ''Rhynchospora'' into subgenera ''Diplostylae'' and ''Haplostylae'', and this classification is still widely used today.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":8" />

The result of this contention is that many ''Rhynchospora'' species have numerous [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]]. Those for ''R. alba'' include ''Dichromena alba''<ref>{{Cite journal|last=MacBride|first=J.F.|date=1929|title=The Status of ''Rhynchospora'': Some Peruvian Sedges|journal=Publication of Field Museum of Natural History, Botanical Series.|volume=4|issue=7|pages=165–66}}</ref> and ''Phaecocacephalum album'',<ref>{{Cite journal|last=House|first=H.D.|date=1920|title=A Consideration of Certain Genera Proposed by Ehrhart.|journal=The American Midland Naturalist|volume=6|issue=9|pages=201–202|doi=10.2307/2992937|jstor=2992937}}</ref> from attempts to rename all ''Rhynchospora''. These synonyms were identified in [[monograph]]s by Kükenthal and Gale,<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":8" /> as well as more recent studies by [[Kew Gardens|Kew]]'s [[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]].<ref name=":12" />

Many [[variety (botany)|varieties]] and forms of ''R. alba'' have also been described over the last two centuries.<ref name=":12" /> Some have subsequently been described as new species – ''R. alba'' var. ''fusca'' was subsequently reclassified as [[Rhynchospora fusca|''R. fusca'']] as it was found to have very different morphology.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Hortus Kewensis|last=Aiton|first=W.T.|year=1810|pages=127}}</ref> Others, such as ''R. alba'' var ''kiusiana'' and ''R. alba'' f. ''laeviseta,'' are considered synonyms,<ref name=":12" /> pending more work on the [[Population genetics|genetic structuring]] of the species.

=== Insights from molecular phylogeny ===
Before [[Sequencing|molecular data]] was more readily available, classification systems such as that of Kükenthal placed ''R. alba'' within ''Rhynchospora'' subg. ''Diplostylae'' based on its tubercle and bifid style.<ref name=":8" /> How the [[Tribe (biology)|tribe]] Rhynchosporae was related to other groups within the [[Cyperaceae]] was less clear, with Kükenthal suggesting they formed their own [[clade]],<ref name=":8" /> others suggesting they were part of the larger Cyperaceae tribe Schoenae.<ref name=":15" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bruhl|first=J.J.|date=1995|title=Sedge genera of the world: relationships and a new classification of the Cyperaceae.|journal=Austral. Syst. Bot.|volume=8|issue=2|pages=125–305|doi=10.1071/SB9950125}}</ref>

A recent [[Molecular phylogenetics|molecular phylogeny]] suggests that Rhynchosporae are a separate but closely related clade to the Schoenae.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mussaya|first1=A.M.|last2=Simpson|first2=D.A.|last3=Verboorn|first3=G.A.|last4=Goetghebeur|first4=P.|last5=Naczi|first5=R.F.C.|last6=Chase|first6=M.W.|last7=Smets|first7=E.|date=2009|title=Phylogeny of Cyperaceae Based on DNA Sequence Data: Current Progress and Future Prospects.|journal=Botanical Review|volume=75|issue=1|pages=20–22}}</ref> Molecular studies within the Rhynchosporae, however, reveal that Kükenthal's widely accepted classification holds less well – neither ''Haplostylae'' nor ''Diplostylae'' are [[Monophyly|monophyletic]], and there appear to be multiple conversions between bifid and non-bifid styles throughout the genus.<ref name=":15" />

Surprisingly, the genus ''Pleurostachys'' (Group I) was also nested within ''Rhynchospora'' rather than sister to it.<ref name=":15" /> Further study is required to confirm the position of ''Pleurostachys,'' but this indicates that ''Rhynchospora'' is not monophyletic, and reclassification of both genera may be necessary.

==Uses==
White beak-sedge is used very little by humans due to its favoured habitat of nutrient-poor acidic bogs,<ref name=":0" /> but is sometimes used as an ornamental plant in the [[United Kingdom|UK]], and in bog [[Restoration ecology|restoration]].<ref name=":11" />

==Conservation status==
''Rhynchospora alba'' is currently assessed by [[International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] as [[least concern]], as it is widespread and "[[habitat]] loss and degradation is not occurring at a scale to qualify the species for a [[Threatened species|threatened]] or [[Near-threatened species|near threatened]] category".<ref name=":11" /> On a regional scale, however, it is threatened by land conversion and over grazing in [[Central Europe|Central]] and [[Eastern Europe]]. It is currently threatened in [[Switzerland]], [[critically endangered]] in [[Croatia]] and has been reported as [[Extinction|extinct]] in [[Hungary]].<ref name=":11" />

There has been little study into the [[Population genetics|genetic structuring]] and threat status of the different varieties of ''Rhynchospora alba''. As such, it is not known if regional population declines are eroding genetic and subspecies diversity, nor whether some sections of the species range are of greater [[Conservation biology|conservation]] concern than others.
